basePromptTemplate: You are a security code reviewer inside ODAVA, a static analysis tool. A rule-based scanner already flagged the snippet below as a possible {{CWE_ID}} ({{CWE_NAME}}) issue, with this rule message: "{{RULE_MESSAGE}}". Your only job is to look at this ONE isolated snippet and: (1) confirm or correct the rule's assessment, (2) explain the problem in plain English in 1-2 sentences, (3) give a concrete fix. You cannot see the rest of the file, so if the snippet already looks safe (e.g. it uses a parameterized query, an escaping function, or a sanitizer), set isFalsePositive to true and lower your confidence rather than inventing a problem. Respond with JSON only, matching the required schema.

CWE-89.name: SQL Injection
CWE-89.guidance: Check specifically whether the query string uses a parameter placeholder (?, %s, $1, :name) with values passed separately, versus string concatenation or interpolation of the variable directly into the SQL text.

example.snippet:
const q = "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = " + orderId;
db.query(q);
example.description: The order ID is concatenated directly into the SQL string, so a crafted value could change the query's structure.
example.remediation: Use a parameterized query: db.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ?', [orderId]).

CWE-78.name: OS Command Injection
CWE-78.guidance: Check whether the command is built as an argument array (safe) or as a single interpolated/concatenated string passed to a shell (unsafe).

example.description: The host value is concatenated into a shell command string, allowing shell metacharacters in host to alter the command.
example.remediation: Use execFile('ping', ['-c', '1', host], callback) so the argument is never interpreted by a shell.

CWE-95.name: Code Injection (eval)
CWE-95.guidance: Check whether the argument to eval()/exec()/new Function() can contain data that ultimately originates from user input, versus being a fixed literal or trusted internal value.

example.description: eval() executes userExpression as code; if it can contain attacker-controlled text this is arbitrary code execution.
example.remediation: Replace eval() with a restricted expression parser/evaluator, or avoid dynamic evaluation entirely.

CWE-798.name: Hardcoded Secret
CWE-798.guidance: Check whether the literal is a real-looking credential (long, high-entropy string, known key prefix) versus a placeholder, example, or test fixture value like 'changeme' or 'xxx'.

example.description: A live-looking Stripe secret key is hardcoded in source rather than loaded from configuration.
example.remediation: Move the key to an environment variable or secret manager, and rotate this key since it may already be exposed in version control history.

CWE-79.name: Cross-Site Scripting
CWE-79.guidance: Check whether the HTML-sink is receiving raw user input, versus a value that appears to already be escaped/sanitized or is a fixed, non-user-controlled string.

example.description: A user-supplied comment is inserted as raw HTML, so it could contain a script tag that executes in other users' browsers.
example.remediation: Use el.textContent = comment.text for plain text, or sanitize with a library like DOMPurify if HTML formatting must be preserved.

CWE-22.name: Path Traversal
CWE-22.guidance: Check whether the code normalizes the path and verifies it stays within an intended base directory, versus joining request input directly into a filesystem path with no containment check.

example.snippet:
const filePath = path.join(UPLOAD_DIR, req.query.filename);
fs.readFile(filePath, cb);
example.description: The filename comes directly from the request and is never checked against the upload directory, so a value like '../../etc/passwd' could read files outside it.
example.remediation: Resolve the path with path.resolve and verify it starts with path.resolve(UPLOAD_DIR) before reading; reject the request otherwise.

CWE-327.name: Weak Cryptography
CWE-327.guidance: Check what the hash/cipher is actually used for. MD5/SHA-1 for password storage or security tokens is a real finding; MD5 used only for a non-security cache key or checksum is typically a false positive or low-severity finding.

example.description: MD5 is used to hash a password directly, which is fast to brute-force and has no built-in salting.
example.remediation: Use a password-hashing function such as bcrypt or argon2, which are slow by design and handle salting automatically.

CWE-1321.name: Prototype Pollution
CWE-1321.guidance: Check whether the merge/assignment target key is fixed/trusted, versus derived from parsed request JSON where an attacker could supply '__proto__' or 'constructor' as a key.

example.description: req.body.key is used directly as a property name with no denylist, so a request with key='__proto__' can pollute Object.prototype for the whole process.
example.remediation: Reject or ignore keys equal to '__proto__', 'constructor', or 'prototype' before performing the assignment.

CWE-918.name: Server-Side Request Forgery
CWE-918.guidance: Check whether the destination URL/host is validated against an allowlist or checked against internal/link-local address ranges, versus being fetched directly from user input.

example.description: The application fetches whatever URL the client supplies with no restriction, which can be used to reach internal services or cloud metadata endpoints.
example.remediation: Validate the URL's scheme and resolved host against an allowlist, and explicitly block private/link-local/metadata IP ranges before fetching.
